prompt: [Synonym] STERN
explanation: A stern teacher holds people to the rule and does not bend, which is what "strict" names. "Gloomy" describes a mood rather than a standard; "formal" describes manners rather than severity; "weary" describes how tired someone is. All four could be said of the same face, but only one says that the rule will be enforced.
distractor_rationales: gloomy — same-semantic-field associate: a stern expression looks unhappy, but the word reports severity, not sadness
formal — same-semantic-field associate: stiffness of manner, which stern faces often have but is not what stern means
weary — same-field associate drawn from the same unsmiling look

prompt: [Synonym] VAST
explanation: Vast reports size and nothing else, so "enormous" is the match. "Empty" reports what is in a space rather than how big it is; "distant" reports how far away it lies; "ancient" reports its age. A vast hall can be crowded, near at hand, and newly built.
distractor_rationales: empty — same-semantic-field associate: the stock phrase "vast emptiness" supplies it
distant — same-field associate from descriptions of vast landscapes
ancient — same-field associate from descriptions of vast ruins

prompt: [Synonym] SUMMON
explanation: To summon someone is to call that person to come, which "call" names directly. "Dismiss" is the opposite instruction; "escort" is walking beside someone who is already coming; "obey" is what the person summoned may then do.
distractor_rationales: dismiss — antonym of the stem, which catches half-remembered vocabulary
escort — same-semantic-field associate from the same scene of being sent for
obey — same-field associate: the response to a summons, not the summons

prompt: [Synonym] WITHER
explanation: To wither is to dry and shrink, which is exactly "shrivel." "Darken" and "harden" are other things a dying leaf may also do, and "scatter" is what happens to it afterward; none of the three carries the drawing-in that the stem requires.
distractor_rationales: scatter — same-semantic-field associate from the same scene of dead leaves
darken — same-field associate: a change that accompanies withering without being it
harden — same-field associate of drying, but a withered stem may stay limp

prompt: [Synonym] PRECARIOUS
explanation: Something precarious is held in place so poorly that it may go over at any moment, which "unsteady" names. "Valuable" answers a different question entirely, "hurried" reports speed, and "stubborn" reports a refusal to move — nearly the opposite of a thing about to slip.
distractor_rationales: valuable — look-alike/sound-alike: precarious against precious
hurried — same-field associate of danger and haste
stubborn — near-antonym: a thing that will not budge is the opposite of one barely holding

prompt: [Synonym] RESOLUTE
explanation: A resolute person has settled on a course and will not be talked off it, which is what "determined" names. "Confused" is the opposite condition, "solitary" reports who is present rather than how firmly one has decided, and "cheerful" reports mood.
distractor_rationales: confused — antonym of the stem: the mind not made up
solitary — look-alike/sound-alike of resolute, and the two are often paired in descriptions of lone figures
cheerful — same-field associate from character description, wrong dimension

prompt: [Synonym] OMINOUS
explanation: An ominous sky warns of harm on the way, which "threatening" names precisely. "Mysterious" says only that something is not understood, "sudden" reports timing, and "unpleasant" is too weak and says nothing about what is coming next.
distractor_rationales: mysterious — same-semantic-field associate: the same atmosphere, no warning of harm
sudden — same-field associate from descriptions of storms, wrong dimension
unpleasant — right polarity, wrong intensity, and lacks the forward-looking sense

prompt: [Synonym] DETER
explanation: To deter is to put someone off doing a thing, which is "discourage." "Delay" only postpones the act, "mislead" sends someone the wrong way while they keep going, and "destroy" acts on the thing rather than on the person's willingness.
distractor_rationales: delay — look-alike/sound-alike: deter against defer
mislead — same-semantic-field associate from the field of turning someone aside
destroy — look-alike/sound-alike: deter against deteriorate, plus shared negative field

prompt: [Synonym] FLIPPANT
explanation: A flippant answer treats a serious matter as a joke, and "disrespectful" names that failure to give the matter its weight. "Talkative" reports quantity of speech rather than its attitude, "apprehensive" reports fear, and "clumsy" reports awkwardness — a flippant remark is usually quick and deft.
distractor_rationales: apprehensive — same-field associate of behavior under questioning; also a register-matched decoy
talkative — same-semantic-field associate: manner of speech, wrong attribute
clumsy — near-antonym in effect, since flippancy is typically nimble rather than awkward

prompt: [Synonym] ABSTAIN
explanation: To abstain is to hold back from doing something, which is what "refrain" names. "Object" is to speak against a thing, which is doing something rather than holding back; "depart" is to leave; "conceal" is to hide.
distractor_rationales: object — same-semantic-field associate: the voting sense of abstain sits beside objecting, but they are opposite acts
depart — same-field associate: leaving the room is how abstaining often looks
conceal — same-field associate of keeping something back, wrong object

prompt: [Synonym] TEMPER
explanation: Students know "temper" as the noun for anger and reach for a word from that field. As a verb it means to soften or tone something down — a judge tempers justice with mercy. "Moderate" names that softening. "Enrage" and "provoke" belong to the primary sense's field and both push the opposite way; "polish" is a finishing step rather than a lessening.
distractor_rationales: enrage — the stem's OTHER meaning: the anger noun, planted as the primary-sense field-mate
provoke — second trap from the same anger field
polish — same-field associate from the craft sense of working a material

prompt: [Synonym] COIN
explanation: The familiar sense sends students to the money field, where three of these choices sit. As a verb, to coin is to make something new — one coins a phrase, a nickname, a term — so "invent" is the match. "Borrow" is close to the opposite, since a borrowed phrase is one nobody coined.
distractor_rationales: borrow — the stem's OTHER meaning: money field, and an antonym of inventing a term
spend — money-field associate of the primary sense
hoard — money-field associate of the primary sense

prompt: [Synonym] STEEP
explanation: Almost everyone meets "steep" first as the adjective for a sharp slope, and "climb" and "sharpen" are planted for that reading. The verb means to let something sit in liquid — tea steeps, and a scholar is steeped in his subject — so "soak" is the synonym. Note that neither "climb" nor "sharpen" is a synonym of the slope sense either; they are associates of it.
distractor_rationales: climb — the stem's OTHER meaning: an associate of the steep-slope sense
harden — same-field associate of what long immersion is imagined to do
sharpen — second associate of the slope sense (a steep, sharp rise)

prompt: [Synonym] PERFUNCTORY
explanation: A perfunctory inspection is gone through only to say it was done, and "cursory" names that hurried, surface treatment. "Punctilious" and "thorough" both describe the careful attention perfunctory work withholds, and "courteous" borrows from the sound of the word rather than its sense — a perfunctory greeting is polite and empty at once.
distractor_rationales: punctilious — antonym of the stem, and a register-matched decoy so the key is not the only advanced word
thorough — antonym of the stem, which catches half-remembered vocabulary
courteous — look-alike/sound-alike: perfunctory against courtesy, plus the same-field association with formulaic politeness

prompt: [Sentence Completion] Because the bus broke down twice on the mountain road, the team's arrival at the tournament was badly -------.
explanation: The cue is "Because": two breakdowns are a cause, and the blank must name their effect on an arrival. Breakdowns cost time, so the arrival is delayed. "Badly" confirms the effect is unwelcome.
distractor_rationales: improved — wrong polarity: a positive word where the cause forces a negative one
announced — fits the topic of a team arriving but has no causal link to a breakdown
shortened — a time word, so it fits the topic, but it reverses the effect a breakdown has on a journey

prompt: [Sentence Completion] Although the puzzle looked ------- at first glance, Omar had it finished before the kettle boiled.
explanation: "Although" sets the first impression against the outcome. Finishing in a few minutes is easy, so the first impression must have been the opposite: the puzzle looked difficult.
distractor_rationales: colorful — fits the topic of a puzzle but stands in no contrast to finishing quickly
expensive — topic-plausible, no logical relation to speed of solving
familiar — would fit if the cue were continuation rather than contrast; a familiar puzzle finished fast is no surprise at all

prompt: [Sentence Completion] A ------- reader, Priya went through four novels in the single week between terms.
explanation: The opening phrase is a definition-in-apposition: the blank must be the adjective the rest of the sentence illustrates. Four novels in one week describes someone who reads and keeps reading, which is "tireless."
distractor_rationales: reluctant — antonym of what the evidence shows; catches students who read only the blank
cautious — a real reading habit, but a cautious reader is a slow one, which the week contradicts
forgetful — topic-adjacent (a reader's memory) but unrelated to the quantity given

prompt: [Sentence Completion] Although the storm had been forecast for a full week, the harbor's preparations were oddly -------, and three boats were lost in a single night.
explanation: "Although" sets a week of warning against what was actually done, and "oddly" marks the result as not what the warning should have produced. The three lost boats fix the direction: the preparations were haphazard.
distractor_rationales: thorough — fits the topic of harbor preparation but violates the contrast cue and cannot explain the lost boats
early — what a week's forecast would normally produce; it satisfies the topic and breaks the "although"
expensive — topic-plausible, but cost stands in no contrast to advance warning

prompt: [Sentence Completion] Because every witness described the car's color differently, the inspector treated their accounts as ------- and went looking for physical evidence instead.
explanation: The cue is "Because," and the consequence is that she stops using the accounts. Testimony that contradicts itself on a plain fact cannot be trusted, so "unreliable" is what the logic forces.
distractor_rationales: deliberate — supplies a motive the sentence never raises; disagreement is not evidence of intent
exhaustive — fits the topic of witness statements but would be a reason to keep using them, not to abandon them
official — topic vocabulary from an investigation, with no causal tie to the disagreement

prompt: [Sentence Completion] Hana rewrote the opening paragraph eleven times and was still not satisfied with it; her standards for her own work were nothing if not -------.
explanation: The semicolon signals continuation: the second clause names the trait the first clause demonstrates. Eleven rewrites and continued dissatisfaction show a standard that is high and will not be talked down, which is "exacting."
distractor_rationales: modest — antonym of the demonstrated trait
flexible — right that she keeps changing the text, wrong about the standard, which never bends
shifting — the attractive trap: the paragraph shifts, but the sentence attributes the trait to her standards, and those are constant

prompt: [Sentence Completion] The pamphlet was -------: it stated its case in nine lines and then simply stopped.
explanation: The colon introduces a definition of the blank. Nine lines and a full stop describe writing that says its piece and no more, which is "terse."
distractor_rationales: ornate — a real style word, but ornamentation is what nine lines rule out
cautious — right register and topic; a pamphlet may be cautious at any length, so the evidence does not select it
rambling — antonym of the definition given after the colon

prompt: [Sentence Completion] The new dam has not made the valley's floods -------; it has merely made them arrive on a schedule the farmers can plan around.
explanation: "Has not made ... ; it has merely made ..." divides what the dam failed to do from what it did. What it did is regulate timing, so the blank must be something else — a change in how OFTEN the floods come. "Rarer" is that word.
distractor_rationales: destructive — wrong direction: the sentence is about a benefit withheld, not harm caused
seasonal — the strongest trap: it fits the topic and is exactly what the dam DID do, so placing it after "has not made" contradicts the second clause
worse — same wrong direction as "destructive"; attractive only if "merely" is read as concessive praise

prompt: [Sentence Completion] Once the pond froze over in November and stayed frozen, the fish beneath the ice grew -------, moving hardly at all until the spring thaw.
explanation: The phrase after the comma defines the blank: "moving hardly at all" is sluggishness. The freeze is the cause and the near-stillness the effect.
distractor_rationales: frantic — antonym of the definition supplied by the following phrase
numerous — fits the topic of fish but reports quantity, not movement, and the sentence gives no count
visible — topic-plausible under clear ice, but unrelated to the stated near-stillness

prompt: [Sentence Completion] The lecture was ------- in its detail yet ------- in its conclusions, so the audience left well informed and still unsure what to think.
explanation: The result clause fixes both blanks. "Well informed" requires detail that was plentiful, so blank one is "rich"; "still unsure what to think" requires conclusions that were not pressed, so blank two is "tentative." The "yet" confirms the two blanks pull against each other.
distractor_rationales: thin .. tentative — the second word fits; the first fails, since thin detail cannot leave an audience well informed
muddled .. bold — fails both: muddled detail does not inform, and bold conclusions would settle the question
rich .. forceful — the first word fits perfectly and the second breaks the sentence: forceful conclusions contradict "still unsure what to think"

prompt: [Sentence Completion] Three rejections in one month left Guerrero anything but -------: he posted the manuscript to a fourth publisher the same afternoon.
explanation: "Anything but" reverses the blank. Posting the manuscript again within hours shows he was NOT put off, so the blank names the state he escaped: discouraged. Readers who skim past the operator supply the state he was in and choose "emboldened," which the sentence then denies.
distractor_rationales: offended — a real response to rejection, but the evidence given is about persistence, not about taking offense
delayed — contradicted only loosely; he acted the same afternoon, yet "delayed" describes the manuscript rather than the man, and the frame asks for his state
emboldened — the operator trap: exactly what he WAS, and therefore wrong after "anything but"

prompt: [Sentence Completion] The footbridge repair, which the council had declared urgent back in March, was all but ------- by September: the crew had one railing left to bolt down.
explanation: "All but" means "very nearly," and the clause after the colon settles it: one railing left is a job all but finished. The whole first clause is bait for the familiar story of an urgent project left undone, which is what "abandoned" sells.
distractor_rationales: funded — topic vocabulary from council works; the colon clause says nothing about money
begun — would make the colon clause absurd, since one railing remaining is the end of the work, not its start
abandoned — the operator trap: readers who take "all but" as "anything except" get a neglected project, which the March urgency primes them to expect

prompt: [Sentence Completion] Although the museum's audio guide was widely praised as -------, visitors who followed it through all nine rooms found that it left the paintings' most puzzling features -------.
explanation: "Although" requires praise in blank one and a shortfall in blank two. "Thorough .. unexplained" gives both: praised as thorough, yet silent on the hard parts. Two pairs survive the first blank, and only testing the second word separates them.
distractor_rationales: superficial .. examined — fails blank one, since no guide is praised as superficial, and reverses blank two as well
meandering .. clear — fails blank one for the same reason, and "left the features clear" would be praise, not a complaint
exhaustive .. discussed — passes blank one perfectly and fails blank two: leaving the features discussed is no criticism, so the "although" collapses

prompt: [Sentence Completion] The coach's praise was ------- but never -------: every player heard it at some point in the season, and no one ever heard it for work he had not actually done.
explanation: The two clauses after the colon fill the two blanks in order. "Every player heard it" gives blank one: frequent. "No one ever heard it for work he had not done" gives blank two, under the "never": unearned. Three pairs offer a defensible first word, so the item turns on the second.
distractor_rationales: rare .. generous — fails blank one, which "every player heard it" rules out
constant .. sincere — passes blank one and fails blank two: "never sincere" contradicts the second clause, which shows the praise was always deserved
frequent .. specific — passes blank one and fails blank two: nothing in the sentence says the praise was vague, and "never specific" would be a criticism the second clause does not support
